walkthroughs.body_html:
Events are independent when one does NOT change the chance of the other.

Examples: tossing a coin twice, rolling two dice, picking a card and putting it back.

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

So P(two heads on two coins) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

A tree diagram shows every outcome of two (or more) trials. Each branch carries a probability.

Multiply along branches to find the probability of a path.

Add path totals if a question asks for more than one path (e.g. "exactly one head").

Tip: probabilities on branches from the same point should add to 1.

If you pick an item, look at it, and put it back, the bag is unchanged for the next pick. So probabilities stay the same.

Example: a bag has 4 red and 6 blue counters. Pick one, replace it, pick again.

P(red then red) = 4/10 × 4/10 = 16/100 = 4/25.

mcqs.q: For two INDEPENDENT events A and B, P(A and B) equals.
options: P(A) + P(B)
P(A) × P(B)
P(A) − P(B)
P(A) ÷ P(B)

mcqs.q: On a tree diagram, to find the probability of a single path you.
options: Add along the branches
Multiply along the branches
Subtract along the branches
Divide along the branches

mcqs.q: If you've flipped a fair coin and got heads 5 times in a row, what is the probability the next flip is heads?
options: 1/2 — each flip is independent of the previous ones.
Less than 1/2, because the coin is 'due' to land on tails to balance the results.
1 because the coin has clearly been biased by the previous flips.
Yes, but only when the probabilities are equal.

mcqs.q: Are 'independent events' and 'mutually exclusive events' the same?
options: No — independent events do not affect each other's probability; mutually exclusive events cannot both happen.
Yes — both mean the events are unrelated.
Yes, but only when the probabilities are equal.
1 because the coin has clearly been biased by the previous flips.

mcqs.q: On a probability tree, how do you find the probability of a sequence of outcomes along one path?
options: Multiply the probabilities along that path.
Yes, but only when the probabilities are equal.
Take the average of the probabilities on the branches.
Add the probabilities along the path.
